subtopics.name: Linked List Fundamentals and Concepts
subtopics.content: A Linked List is a linear data structure where elements are stored in nodes. Each node contains data and a reference (pointer) to the next node in the sequence. Unlike arrays, linked lists do not store elements in contiguous memory locations, which allows dynamic memory allocation and efficient insertions and deletions.

subtopics.name: Insertion Operations in Linked Lists
subtopics.content: Insertion in a linked list involves adding a new node into the list. Nodes can be inserted at the beginning, end, or any specific position. Since linked lists do not require shifting elements like arrays, insertion operations are efficient and mainly involve adjusting node pointers.

subtopics.name: Deletion Operations in Linked Lists
subtopics.content: Deletion in a linked list removes a node from the structure by updating the pointer of the previous node to skip the node being deleted. Deletions can happen at the beginning, end, or at a specific position. Proper pointer updates are essential to maintain the structure of the list.

subtopics.name: Searching and Utility Operations
subtopics.content: Searching and utility operations help perform common tasks on linked lists such as traversing the list, searching for a value, counting nodes, finding the middle node, and retrieving the nth node from the end. These operations help understand traversal logic and pointer manipulation.

subtopics.name: Reversal and Two Pointer Techniques
subtopics.content: Reversing a linked list is a common problem where the direction of node pointers is changed so the last node becomes the head. Two-pointer techniques such as slow and fast pointers are widely used for solving problems like detecting cycles, finding middle nodes, and removing nodes from the end.

subtopics.name: Linked List Variants & Advanced Problems
subtopics.content: Linked lists also have different variants such as Doubly Linked Lists and Circular Linked Lists. Doubly linked lists allow traversal in both directions using next and previous pointers, while circular linked lists connect the last node back to the head. Advanced problems include merging sorted linked lists, detecting cycles, checking if a linked list is a palindrome, and finding the intersection of two linked lists.

class Solution:

solutions.code:
class Solution:
    def sortList(self, head):
        if not head or not head.next:
            return head
        # Find middle
        slow, fast = head, head.next
        while fast and fast.next:
            slow = slow.next
            fast = fast.next.next
        mid = slow.next
        slow.next = None
        left = self.sortList(head)
        right = self.sortList(mid)
        # Merge sorted lists
        dummy = ListNode(0)
        curr = dummy
        while left and right:
            if left.val < right.val:
                curr.next = left
                left = left.next
            else:
                curr.next = right
                right = right.next
            curr = curr.next
        curr.next = left if left else right
        return dummy.next

class Solution:
    def sortedListToBST(self, head):
        if not head: return None
        if not head.next: return TreeNode(head.val)
        slow = head
        fast = head
        prev = None
        while fast and fast.next:
            prev = slow
            slow = slow.next
            fast = fast.next.next
        prev.next = None

        root.right = self.sortedListToBST(slow.next)
